Bermuda Grapples with Currency Crisis, Manufacturing Sector Feels the Strain

Bermuda is facing mounting economic turmoil this week as a sudden collapse in the Bermudian dollar’s value has sent shockwaves through the island’s financial and industrial sectors. The crisis, sparked by a rapid devaluation of the local currency against the US dollar, has led to soaring import prices and widespread uncertainty, with companies such as Axalta Coating Systems Ltd reporting significant operational challenges.

The crisis began late last month, when international investors reacted to concerns about Bermuda’s rising public debt and shrinking foreign currency reserves. Over the past ten days, the Bermudian dollar has lost nearly 35% of its value, making imported goods—on which the island is heavily reliant—far more expensive. The Bermuda Chamber of Commerce estimates that wholesale prices for industrial supplies have jumped as much as 40% since the start of June.

“We are seeing a situation where manufacturers simply cannot keep up with the cost fluctuations,” said Sharon Dill, president of the Bermuda Manufacturing Association. “Many of our members are scrambling to secure supplies before prices rise again, or are being forced to delay production altogether.”

Axalta Coating Systems Ltd, a major employer in Bermuda’s industrial coatings sector, confirmed it has been directly impacted by the currency crisis. “The abrupt devaluation has severely disrupted our supply chain and increased the cost of imported raw materials,” said Marc Evans, site manager for Axalta in Hamilton. “We’re taking steps to safeguard local jobs but cannot rule out temporary production slowdowns if conditions persist.”

Export-oriented companies are also feeling the pinch. While a weaker Bermudian dollar would traditionally make Bermudian goods more competitive overseas, the dominance of imported components in local manufacturing means that input costs have risen faster than any gains from favorable exchange rates. According to the Ministry of Economic Development, business confidence among manufacturers has dropped to its lowest level since the global financial crisis of 2008.

Labor groups are raising concerns about job security amid the downturn. “We’ve seen overtime hours cut and some companies moving to four-day workweeks,” said Terrence Fox, secretary of the Bermuda Industrial Workers Union. “Our priority is keeping Bermudians employed as the crisis unfolds.”

The government has announced emergency measures, including talks with international lenders and the introduction of temporary import subsidies for essential goods. However, Finance Minister Eleanor Richards cautioned that “restoring confidence and stability will require time and coordinated action.”

For now, businesses and workers across Bermuda are bracing for further volatility as the currency crisis continues to unfold, with the outlook for the coming months described by one analyst as “highly uncertain.”
